newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters stresses role of longer NZ rates for growth.
newsitem.headline: Peters stresses role of longer NZ rates for growth.

text.p: New Zealand's Treasurer Winston Peters on Wednesday deflected questions about the potential damage to the country's growth prospects that could follow a recent sharp jump in short-term interest rates by saying long-term interest rates were important.
These long rates, typically measured by government bond yields, have been largely stable in recent weeks.

Asked if he was concerned that recent rises in short-dated interest rates would slow the economy and hurt its growth prospects, he told reporters, "You have to look at long term interest rates -- they haven't moved at all."
Peters was speaking after appearing at a routine hearing of Parliament's Finance and Expenditure select committee, at which he was questioned repeatedly about growth prospects.

MPs emphasised that many private sector economists did not share the Treasury's mid-range growth forecasts, partly in the light of recent weak economic indicators and after a jump in short-term rates that has accompanied a recent dollar slide.
Peters said he stood by the Treasury forecasts, and disagreed when later asked if recent current account and inflation data implied its expectations were too optimistic.
"That data doesn't suggest that," he told reporters.

When asked to comment on the current mix of market monetary conditions, which are marked by a sharply lower dollar and higher bank bill rates than a few weeks ago, Peters said, "I have a view, but it's not one that I'm going to express".
Asked if he could comment on the impact on the economy of higher rates and a lower dollar, he said: "It is something a number of people have been asking for for a long time."
One MP asked him how he felt about the prospect of the country's current account deficit rising towards 5.5 percent by March 1999, as treasury predicted in the budget.
"We are not oblivious to it. We have to look at the international market and see what their judgement is," he added.
Peters noted that rating agency S&P had said on several occasions that it was aware of the situation and accepted the forecast level as unlikely to have an impact on New Zealand's rating prospects.
